subtitle: The unglamorous 80% of every data project, written down: take messy real-world PDFs and land them as validated, cleaned, well-chunked datasets your stack can actually use
audience: Developers handed a folder of PDFs (manuals, reports, invoices, papers) and told to 'load it into the system'. No ML background needed — just JavaScript fundamentals and willingness to stare at ugly text. Every algorithm in this course (routing, cleaning, validation, chunking, TF-IDF retrieval checks) runs live in the JS Playground; PDF-library calls target your own Node project.
outcomes: Classify any PDF as text-native, scanned, or hybrid — and route each class to the right extraction path
Extract text with correct reading order and repair the standard damage (hyphenation, headers/footers, ligatures, whitespace)
Design a target schema for extracted data and validate rows against it with readable error reports
Run the cleanup cookbook: unicode normalization, mojibake detection, date/number standardization, key-based dedup
Chunk documents with overlap and page metadata for downstream retrieval, and measure chunk quality with a TF-IDF sanity check
Assemble the full loader pipeline (route → extract → validate → clean → chunk → evaluate) and report its reject rate honestly

assessment.q: A PDF renders perfect text on screen but getTextContent returns empty strings. Diagnosis?
options: Scanned/image-only PDF: pixels, not text — route to OCR, not text extraction
assessment.explain: Rendering proves pixels exist; extraction needs a text layer. Screen appearance says nothing about extractability — triage by layer presence (selectable text? embedded fonts?), not by looks (Ch.1).

assessment.q: Extracted words read 'cus- tomer', 'fi-nance' at line ends. Fix?
options: Dehyphenate: rejoin letter-hyphen-newline-letter sequences; keep real compound hyphens (mid-line, spaced, or capitalized continuations)
assessment.explain: End-of-line hyphen + lowercase continuation = line-break artifact; mid-line hyphens are usually real. Blanket deletion corrupts compound words (Ch.2).

assessment.q: Why validate against a schema instead of cleaning harder?
options: Validation separates interpretation (what shape must hold) from repair (fixing values) — rejects get quarantined with reasons instead of silently corrupting downstream
assessment.explain: No amount of cleaning fixes a row missing its key field. Schema-first means rejects carry reasons; clean-first means garbage enters quietly (Ch.3).

assessment.q: Text shows 'MÃ¼ller' and 'â€”'. Diagnosis and first action?
options: Mojibake (double-encoded UTF-8): detect via replacement chars/signature sequences, then re-decode from the original bytes — never regex away the symptoms
assessment.explain: MÃ¼ = UTF-8 bytes misread as Latin-1. Repair means returning to bytes and decoding correctly; character-level patching destroys information (Ch.4).

assessment.q: Two rows share an email key with different names. Dedup decision?
options: Never auto-merge on conflicting keys: quarantine for human review — dedup deletes data, so survivors need provenance (kept id + merged-from log)
assessment.explain: Key collision with conflicting payloads is a human judgment, not an algorithmic one. Auto-merge destroys evidence; quarantine preserves it with reasons (Ch.4).

assessment.q: Chunking with zero overlap for RAG retrieval. Risk?
options: Boundary amnesia: answers spanning a cut become unretrievable as one unit — overlap (10–20%) buys boundary recall at linear storage cost
assessment.explain: Cuts fall mid-thought. Overlap duplicates boundary text so split answers survive as retrievable units; metadata (page spans) makes citations possible (Ch.5).

assessment.q: Your TF-IDF check retrieves the wrong chunk for 'refund policy'. First suspect?
options: Vocabulary mismatch (query says 'refund', chunk says 'reimbursement') or the answer spans a chunk boundary — diagnose before changing chunk size
assessment.explain: Retrieval failures diagnose the pipeline: mismatch vocabulary vs boundary splits vs missing content. The check's value is the diagnosis, not the score (Ch.5).

assessment.q: Loader reports 2% reject rate with reasons. Good or bad?
options: Healthy: a measured, reasoned reject stream proves validation works; 0% means the validators are asleep, 40% means the schema fights reality
Only the rate matters, not reasons
assessment.explain: Reject rate is a process metric with reasons attached: low-but-nonzero with categorized reasons signals a working pipeline. Silence (0%) or floods both demand investigation (Ch.3 + capstone).

project.title: The Manual Loader
project.summary: Pick a real multi-page PDF manual/report in your domain (10+ pages). Build the full OpenDataLoader pipeline — triage, extract, validate, clean, chunk, evaluate — and deliver the loaded dataset plus an honest pipeline report: reject rate with reasons, retrieval hit-rate on 10 hand-written questions, and the three ugliest source artifacts you survived.
requirements: Triage report: PDF class (text/scanned/hybrid) with evidence (layer test results), chosen extraction path per class
Target schema: 5+ fields with types, required flags, and format rules; validation function returning per-row error lists
Cleaned dataset: JSONL, one record per chunk with text, page_start, page_end, source label; NFKC-normalized, dehyphenated, dated-standardized
Chunking: fixed budget (e.g. ~500 chars) with ~15% overlap; no chunk crosses a section boundary silently (record boundary decisions)
Retrieval check: 10 hand-written questions against the chunks via TF-IDF/cosine; report hit-rate (gold chunk in top-3) with per-question verdicts
Pipeline report: stage counts in/out, reject rate with categorized reasons, the three ugliest artifacts, and what you would fix with one more day
technical: All algorithms (routing, cleaning, validation, chunking, TF-IDF) run in the JS Playground or plain Node — no new dependencies required for the core
PDF-library calls (pdf.js/Tesseract) run in your own Node project; playground code uses representative extracted text
Every number reproducible: fixer seeds committed, chunker parameters recorded, gold answers committed alongside questions
Rejects preserved with reasons — never silently dropped
project.architecture: Four sections: (1) Source dossier — triage evidence and path choices; (2) Pipeline — per-stage in/out counts, schema, and the validation/quarantine design; (3) Retrieval evaluation — 10 questions, verdicts, hit-rate, failure diagnoses; (4) Honest report — reject taxonomy, ugliest artifacts, one-more-day fixes.
steps: Triage the PDF: layer tests, class decision, extraction path per class
Extract raw text (library in Node) and paste representative pages into playground snippets
Write the schema + validator; run it over extracted rows; tune rules from the reject stream
Apply the cleanup cookbook in fixed order (normalize → dehyphenate → strip furniture → standardize → dedupe)
Chunk with overlap + metadata; run the TF-IDF check on 10 questions; diagnose every miss
Assemble the report; lead with the reject rate and the retrieval hit-rate, not adjectives
evaluation: Schema enforced with per-row errors; rejects categorized with reasons and counts
Ch overlap present with page metadata; no silent section-boundary crossings
10 questions with gold chunks; hit-rate computed and every miss diagnosed
Three ugliest artifacts documented with the fix applied
Numbers reproducible from committed code + parameters
stretch: Add table extraction for one real table (cell grid → rows) with a validation rule per column
OCR one scanned page with Tesseract.js and report character-level diffs vs expectations
Swap TF-IDF for an embeddings provider on 3 questions and compare verdicts with cost noted

interviewQs.q: Text looks perfect on screen but extracts as garbage. Walk me through triage.
interviewQs.a: Screen rendering proves pixels, not text layers. Triage: (1) selectable text? extract a page and inspect raw strings — empty/garbled means missing/broken text layer; (2) embedded fonts present? custom encodings without ToUnicode maps extract as mojibake-by-construction; (3) scanned? route to OCR. Each answer picks the path: text layer → pdf.js-style extraction with cleanup; broken encoding → OCR or mapping repair; scans → Tesseract with preprocessing. Never re-run the same extractor hoping — classify first, then route.

interviewQs.q: Dehyphenation: how do you rejoin line breaks without corrupting real hyphens?
interviewQs.a: Rule on shape: rejoin only letter-hyphen-newline-lowercase-letter (line-break artifact); preserve mid-line hyphens, spaced dashes, and hyphen-newline-capitalized (likely genuine compounds or proper nouns). Then verify on samples: over-eager joining corrupts 'state-of-the-art' split across lines only if you ignore the lowercase-continuation signal. Report the rule with examples — cleanup without stated rules is unreviewable.

interviewQs.q: Validate-first vs clean-first: defend your order.
interviewQs.a: Validate-first: schema defines acceptable shape, rejects quarantine with reasons, cleaning operates on known-good structures. Clean-first risks laundering garbage into plausible-looking rows (a 'fixed' date that was actually a page number). The pipeline order is route → extract → validate → clean → chunk: interpretation before repair, repair before use. Reject rate with reasons is the process metric proving it works.

interviewQs.q: Chunk overlap: wasteful duplication or necessary? Quantify it.
interviewQs.a: Necessary for boundary recall: answers spanning a cut are unretrievable as units without it. Cost is linear and bounded — 15% overlap on 500-char chunks adds ~15% storage for large recall gains on cross-boundary questions. Measure, don't philosophize: retrieval hit-rate with 0% vs 15% overlap on the same question set decides the parameter per corpus.

interviewQs.q: Your retrieval check fails on 'refund policy' but the text is in the corpus. Debug live.
interviewQs.a: Three suspects in order: (1) vocabulary mismatch — query 'refund' vs chunk 'reimbursement/returns' (TF-IDF has no synonyms; check term overlap directly); (2) boundary split — answer spans two chunks (inspect neighbors, raise overlap); (3) chunk missing — extraction dropped the page (headers/footers strip ate it, or scanned page un-OCRed). Each has a distinct fix: synonym expansion, overlap/boundary rules, extraction repair. The check's job is producing this diagnosis.
